sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09923 (full text read from https://arxiv.org/html/2601.09923v3, v3 dated 04 Jun 2026; v1 and v2 HTML also retrieved and consistent on all coded claims)
statedGuarantee: Control flow integrity (CFI) for a Computer Use Agent: a Privileged Planner (P-LLM) that never observes the environment emits a complete branching plan single-shot before execution; an interpreter runs that plan, invoking a Quarantined Perception model (Q-VLM/Q-LLM) only to resolve runtime values (screen summaries, UI coordinates, boolean state verdicts) that are bound to plan variables. The claim is that the set of calls executed, their order, and the conditional logic selecting among them are fixed entirely by the planner, so an adversary who controls rendered content cannot inject an action the planner did not write. The paper is explicit that this is CFI ONLY: data-flow security is not claimed, and the authors deliberately omit CaMeL's and Fides' security-policy/capability components. The authors themselves name and demonstrate the residual class, 'Branch Steering', in which manipulated perception outputs route execution down an attacker-preferred but structurally valid branch.
advertisedRhetoric: Title: 'System-level Security for Computer Use Agents'. Abstract: 'Among proposed defenses, architectural isolation provides the strongest guarantees by strictly separating trusted task planning from untrusted environment observations' and 'Single-shot planning ... provides control flow integrity guarantees against arbitrary instruction injections'. Introduction: 'structurally enforcing control flow integrity'; 'Control flow is thus determined entirely by the plan: adversaries cannot inject instructions that deviate from it.'; 'Attackers are restricted to pre-written paths.' Discussion: 'it eliminates the arbitrary-instruction injection class entirely: attacks that introduce actions the planner did not write are structurally impossible under Dual-LLM.' Appendix G: 'Injecting new actions entirely absent from the plan. The attack class CFI is specifically designed to prevent. Structurally impossible regardless of attack technique.' The words 'system-level', 'architectural', 'structural' and 'strongest guarantees' carry the enforcement claim; no cryptographic or OS mechanism is ever named, so the advertised tier is left unclear rather than read up to T2.
tierSpan: Dual-LLM guarantees CFI: branching logic and action sequences are determined entirely by the planner, which never observes the environment. It does not prevent data-flow attacks, where malicious content shapes the Q-LLM’s outputs and thereby the arguments or conditional values that flow through the plan. Prior work addresses data-flow attacks via semantic policies and capabilities, but these require tools with intrinsic meaning; CUA actions like click have none without environmental context, making policy-based protection difficult to deploy.
cheapestDefeat: Worked explicitly. (1) GUARANTEE: every action the agent performs is a step the P-LLM wrote, in the order and under the conditions it wrote. (2) MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the CaMeL-style plan interpreter, an in-process application-layer chokepoint that is the sole actuator - it decodes the plan, calls the Q-VLM, binds returns to plan variables, and issues the GUI tool calls. (3) CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: do not attack the interpreter at all. Place a fake cookie banner inside an ad slot on a page the agent will load, so that a single pre-written find('cookie popup') call returns attacker-chosen coordinates and the pre-written click executes against attacker-chosen UI. No signature is forged, no plan is edited, no code is injected - the interpreter behaves exactly as specified while the effect is attacker-selected. The paper's Appendix G rates this the LOWEST-difficulty goal: 'Requires only a single find call for a predictable UI element (e.g., a cookie popup) on a page the attacker controls, which our one-step cookie attack achieves.' The authors' own strongest configured defense (Multi-Modal Consensus, tuned to prioritize security with high false positive rates) is defeated by their gradient-based pixel attack. (4) TIER OF THE MECHANISM DEFEATED: an application-layer chokepoint whose contract binds only the plan's call graph, not the effect of a click at attacker-supplied pixel coordinates -> T3. Two further reasons the score cannot rise above T3: the chokepoint is semantically empty by the paper's own admission (click 'ha[s] none [no intrinsic meaning] without environmental context'), and once a steered click launches an application or a page, nothing in the architecture mediates that descendant process or its traffic - there is no OS boundary, no sandbox, no netns, no egress allowlist anywhere in the design.
placementSpan: We assume an attacker who cannot access or manipulate the P-LLM but can manipulate parts of the execution environment. This aligns with realistic scenarios where attackers control entire malicious websites or inject content within trusted sites (e.g., advertisements, forum posts, product reviews), but do not control all websites the agent interacts with or the underlying agent infrastructure. The attacker embeds malicious visual or textual cues that the Q-VLM perceives during plan execution, with the goal of manipulating the information returned to the P-LLM and thereby steering the agent into adversary-chosen actions.

coverageSpans.E1: CUA action spaces are broader (spanning OS dialogs and desktop applications) and operate at the visual level (clicks at pixel coordinates), with no equivalent protocol layer to intercept.
coverageSpans.E2: Causing clicks on arbitrary attacker-chosen elements. Requires a pixel attack to survive defenses when the element cannot be obviously spoofed.
coverageSpans.E3: DOM Consistency blocks it on static Google banners via the “Advertisement” frame in the DOM, but fails on HTML5 banners, which replace the advertisement frame with a cookie frame. Multi-Modal Consensus struggles to distinguish fabricated cookie banners from legitimate ones without degrading utility, consistent with weak success rates of prompt-based defenses ( Evtimov et al., 2025 ) .
coverageSpans.E5: Empirically, the unoptimized baseline only succeeds on short, mostly self-contained sequences (e.g., changing a font size, installing a browser extension), and fails on tasks requiring multiple sub-goals or many dependent edits.
coverageSpans.E6: Data exfiltration. Requires an even stronger plan structure: the plan must sequentially include both a read step and a send step (e.g., summarize content, then submit elsewhere), and the attacker must compromise both to extract attacker-chosen content and route it to attacker-controlled destinations. Such plan structures are uncommon outside narrow use cases.
coverageSpans.E7: The P-LLM writes calls to Q-VLM functions at plan time but never observes their return values; the interpreter invokes these calls at execution time and binds the outputs to plan variables consumed by subsequent actions and branches.

schneider.surrogate: Control flow integrity over the plan's call graph: the executed sequence of function calls and the conditional structure selecting among them must correspond to the P-LLM's pre-written, environment-blind plan. This is a safety property - the bad thing (executing a call the plan does not contain, or taking a branch the plan does not define) is a finite-prefix violation an execution monitor sitting in the interpreter can detect and refuse. The paper enforces exactly this, and enforces it well: 'attacks that introduce actions the planner did not write are structurally impossible under Dual-LLM.'
schneider.objective: Security of the agent against prompt injection - that the agent performs only actions the user actually intended. This is not monitorable on a single execution. It requires (a) data-flow / information-flow security, an explicit hyperproperty over how untrusted observations influence action arguments and branch conditions, which the paper concedes it does not provide ('It does not prevent data-flow attacks'), and (b) a semantic interpretation of coordinate-level actions that does not exist ('CUA actions like click have none without environmental context'). The gap between surrogate and objective IS the paper's own Branch Steering result: control flow can be perfectly intact while the agent clicks the attacker's button. Credit where due - the authors name this split themselves rather than letting the CFI surrogate stand in for the injection-security objective.

WHY THIS PAPER MATTERS TO THE T-12 CORPUS, and the correction it forces: the corpus brief flags that the paper 'claims SYSTEM-LEVEL security while a perception model resolves runtime values inside the loop.' The title does say 'System-level Security', and that phrase will mislead a skim-reader into hearing OS enforcement. But this is NOT a paper that hides the gap. It is one of the most honest artifacts in the corpus. The authors name the exact defect the brief points at, give it a name ('Branch Steering'), build two attacks against their own system, and report that BOTH succeed against their strongest defense configured to prioritize security over utility. Sec. 2.2 draws the control-flow / data-flow line explicitly and puts their system on the weak side of it. Any write-up that presents this paper as overclaiming would be wrong on the record; the criticism that survives is narrower and is about VOCABULARY, not honesty - 'system-level' and 'architectural isolation provides the strongest guarantees' are load-bearing words for an interpreter-level chokepoint, and readers will over-read them.

TIER. Scored T3, and there is no serious argument for higher. Nothing cryptographic binds anything (T1 out). No OS, kernel, container, netns, seccomp or firewall mechanism appears anywhere in the design (T2 out) - the paper in fact cites browser-layer sandboxing (CeLLMate) as an EXTERNAL defense its plan could 'compose with', which concedes it does not itself provide one. What remains is the CaMeL plan interpreter: an in-process application chokepoint. This is the worked example in the coding rubric almost verbatim - structural mandates enforced by an in-process interpreter score T3, because defeating the interpreter is unnecessary when the effect can be obtained through a step the interpreter already permits.

A SHARPER POINT THE ADJUDICATOR SHOULD SEE. This chokepoint is unusually weak even for T3, because it is SEMANTICALLY EMPTY. A normal T3 proxy at least knows what passes it (a URL, a filename, a tool name). Here the mediated unit is click(x, y), and the paper says plainly that such actions carry no intrinsic meaning without environmental context - which is also why the authors could not deploy CaMeL's policy layer and deliberately dropped it ('we exclude such policies, so our setup represents a worst-case Dual-LLM security baseline'). So the chokepoint constrains the SHAPE of the action sequence while constraining almost nothing about what the actions DO. That is the transferable lesson for the SoK: mediating a call graph is not mediating an effect, and a mediation layer's strength is bounded by the semantic content of the unit it mediates.

COVERAGE - READ THIS BEFORE DISPUTING THE CELLS. E1-E7 is a coding-agent effector taxonomy; NOVA is a GUI agent whose only actuators are pixel clicks and keystrokes into a desktop VM (OSWorld: Chrome, GIMP, LibreOffice, VS Code, OS tasks). The system names none of E1-E7 as an effector class and has no mechanism aimed at any of them, so the taxonomy scores mostly not-covered per the rule that an unaddressed effector is not-covered, never not-applicable.

I considered and REJECTED a uniform 'partial' across E1-E5. The argument for it is real: CFI does place one weak, uniform bound on every agent-originated effect - an attacker cannot add a step the plan does not contain, so a plan with no save-file step cannot be made to save a file. I rejected it because that bound collapses the moment a plan contains a coordinate-resolved click, which by construction EVERY NOVA plan does (find -> click is the core primitive), and because the paper's own Appendix G rates 'Causing clicks on arbitrary attacker-chosen elements' as an achievable goal requiring only a pixel attack that they demonstrate defeats their strongest defense. Once the adversary can direct a click anywhere on a desktop screen, file writes, application launches and extension installs are all reachable, and none of them are mediated as such. Conservative stance therefore says not-covered for E1, E2, E4, E5, E6. An adjudicator who weighs the plan-shape bound more heavily than I do would move E1/E2/E5 to partial; I flag that as the single most contestable judgment in this coding.

E3 is partial rather than not-covered for a specific, evidenced reason: it is the one effector class the system actually AIMS at. DOM Consistency and Multi-Modal Consensus exist precisely to stop redirection to attacker-controlled sites, and DOM Consistency demonstrably blocks some instances (static Google ad banners, via the Advertisement frame) and demonstrably fails on others (HTML5 banners). That is the textbook definition of partial - reaches some instances and provably not others. It cannot be covered: the covert-channel rule bites (the stated contract excludes data flow, and destination is chosen by data flow), the depth rule bites (a loaded page's own subresource requests - ads, trackers, beacons - are descendant egress that nothing mediates), and the paper's headline attack IS an egress redirection that succeeds.

E7 is partial and is the OTHER judgment call. The only sub-agent-like spawns in the architecture are the Q-VLM / Q-LLM / verifier-model invocations, and those genuinely ARE fixed by the plan and cannot be extended by injected content - a real reach. But it is only partial: any spawn achieved through the GUI (launching another agent or program by click) is entirely outside the interpreter, and in the Fides-NOVA variant the authors relax variable redaction and concede 'execution termination cannot be guaranteed', calling the relaxation 'a security breach in particular', bounded only by the ad-hoc max_steps / max_turn counters. A reasonable adjudicator could argue E7 should be not-covered on the grounds that model invocations are not 'sub-agents' in the taxonomy's intended sense; I took partial per the instruction to prefer partial where coverage is arguable.

E6 note on the rubric's cap: the rule caps E6 at partial when no credential list is published. That is a ceiling, not a floor - here there is no credential mechanism at all, no enumeration, no mediation, so it floors at not-covered. The agent types into login fields with whatever credentials the VM holds, and a steered click can put a phishing page under that typing. What the plan structure DOES bound is exfiltration composition (App. G item 5: a plan lacking a send step cannot send), which makes exfil harder but is not credential-use mediation.

EVIDENCE GRADE L3, self-inflicted. The authors publish two working bypasses of their own system - a cookie-popup prompt injection (one-step, plus multi-step hop-site and long-range variants that evade hyperlink verification) and a gradient-based pixel attack that induces the Q-VLM to emit thought traces and coordinates consistent with the search instruction so that screenshot, DOM and Q-VLM output all look legitimate simultaneously. Both succeed against the strongest redundancy defense. Code is released. This is L3 without needing an outside party.

ADVERSARY PLACEMENT. Primary A2 and it is unambiguous - all testing is content injected into rendered web pages (ad banners, DOM elements, adversarial pixels). Secondary A3 is listed with a caveat the adjudicator should weigh: the DESIGN treats the perception model as untrusted by construction ('Quarantined Perception (Q-VLM): An untrusted Vision-Language Model'), and the pixel attack does induce the perception model itself to lie - but the compromise is environment-mediated, not a poisoned or backdoored checkpoint, so A3 is addressed structurally rather than tested directly. A4 and A5 are explicitly OUT of the threat model ('do not control ... the underlying agent infrastructure'), so they are neither addressed nor tested and are not listed as secondary.

THREE THINGS A HUMAN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD NOT MISS. (i) The strong-attacker assumptions are genuinely strong and stated as such - attacker knows the task, knows the toolset, and can approximately predict the generated plans - which makes the negative results MORE credible, not less. (ii) The security evaluation is restricted to browser tasks ('For tractability we restrict to browser-based tasks') while the utility evaluation spans full OSWorld, so the attack surface of the non-browser desktop applications the agent drives is never tested at all. (iii) Utility numbers are pass@k with oracle selection - 'Pass@k represents an upper bound assuming oracle selection' - and even the undefended Claude baseline (37.7%) is far below its published 58.1% because of a 15-step cap, so the headline '57% retained' is a ratio between two already-depressed numbers and should not be quoted as a deployment-readiness figure.

UNCERTAINTY I COULD NOT RESOLVE. The paper does not describe the interpreter's own interposition point in implementation detail - whether GUI tool calls are issued in-process, over the OSWorld VM boundary, or through a separate driver. Per the conservative stance I treated the interposition point as unproven and scored the guarantee at the tier of the weakest plausible realization (in-process application chokepoint, T3). If the released code turns out to place the actuator behind a genuine OS or VM boundary with an enforced action allowlist, an E1/E2 re-score toward partial would be warranted - but nothing in the prose claims that, and the paper's own framing of browser-layer sandboxing as a future composition partner argues against it.
